paragraphs: In 1895, the Odesa branch of the Imperial Russian Technical Society organized the “Home Improvement Exhibition” at the palace. The exhibition occupied the entire palace building, as well as the upper and lower gardens behind it; in addition, temporary street pavilions were erected. Over the course of its 120-day run, the exhibition was visited by more than 185,000 people.

Exhibitions of technical innovations were very popular during the period of industrialization. At that time, exhibiting at such events served several purposes simultaneously: it served as advertising for manufacturers, an opportunity to win awards, and a platform for exchanging innovations among manufacturers. The exhibition was particularly relevant for Odesa during the 19th-century construction boom, as it promoted the idea of hygienic, functional, and aesthetically pleasing housing.

paragraphs: The “Home Improvement Exhibition” was a major event for the city and differed from exhibitions in other cities of the Russian Empire at that time. Newspapers criticized the Odesa exhibition for displaying works of art, decorative items, and plants, since such exhibitions typically focused exclusively on technological innovations.

It would be difficult to single out a specific theme or idea for each individual hall. For example, in the largest hall on the second floor, alongside Borys Edwards’ bronze sculpture “Shurka,” a grand piano, samples of asphalt, various types of wallpaper, stools, and bookcases were on display. The outdoor section of the exhibition featured a laboratory for testing the strength of materials, restaurants and cafes, separate pavilions for local manufacturers, and an illuminated fountain. On the exhibition plan and in Volodymyr Naake’s drawing, you can see the staircase on the north facade that existed at the time, leading from the palace’s ballroom to the garden.
